cells.tense: Care moves through you here without bracing, and without clutching what's already underway.
cells.act: surrender the outcome and keep the act
cells.ask: Keep up what you do for whatever you're tending that's nearest ready — and somewhere this week, quit checking whether it's working. A night or a day, whichever suits. The care carries on; the tally is what you lay aside.
cells.core:
What's entering your life in this part gets met by someone who can tend it. You make conditions for things to grow in, then step back and let them. That's the whole move, and it's already working — no forcing the pace, no clutching at what's clearly done being yours.

It holds as long as you keep handing over the ending. For that nearest-ready thing, carry on caring for it, and drop the measuring for a stretch — a night without checking, a week without taking its pulse. The doing is yours to keep; the verdict is what you put down. A plant grows whether or not somebody stands over it counting the leaves.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it, and you don't hold it.
cells.verb: tending what is growing before it has to prove itself
cells.place: at the threshold where what is entering meets the room

cells.tense: Care that was patient is pushing ahead, and you are bracing for a future you have already written.
cells.act: sketch the whole of it badly, on one page, and keep the sketch
cells.ask: Take what you're steering into place — a person, a plan, a project — and sketch how you want it to go on one page, roughly, in one sitting. Keep the page, and don't act on it.
cells.core:
When care gets ahead of itself, it shades into steering — holding the shape of someone's unfolding so tightly there's no room left for surprise. You're rehearsing how it should go, and what's arriving gets met with a plan instead of attention. The reach comes from love; it's still a grip.

Some of that forward energy is real, and useful — it just needs somewhere to go other than at the person. Put the whole future you're picturing on paper, badly sketched, one sitting. Keep the page and don't act on it. The picture stops needing to be enforced, and the one you're caring for gets their own timing back.
cells.sheetLine: Your care has started arriving with a plan attached.

cells.tense: Something is arriving while the door has stayed shut, and nothing here grows because nothing is let in.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: Choose something you genuinely want that's been sitting quietly. Then do a single plain thing in its direction this week — a sign-up, a message, showing up once. Not the whole road. A step, no story about why not.
cells.core:
On this side of things, care runs outward and almost nothing gets room to grow in you. Telephones get answered; your own projects don't. The independence is real, and it keeps things at the distance where they can't need anything from you — and you stay out of the room when what's arriving shows up.

The way in isn't to manufacture a feeling. It's to want something on purpose, and take an inch toward it. Choose the one you'd mind most losing, or the one you've avoided because it feels too far. Do one small act in its direction. Nothing has to look like progress — just turn toward it, with the old reasons left where they are.
cells.sheetLine: The door's been shut, and something is still arriving.

cells.tense: You are carrying a great deal you didn't agree to carry, and you are calling it yours.
cells.act: stop holding what no longer serves
cells.ask: There's a duty you keep for someone else that finished — a worry, a role, a job nobody asked you to keep. Tell yourself, quietly, that it's done. Then set it down: hand it back, stop asking after it, leave that piece be.
cells.core:
People near you know exactly what to do with hard things: bring them to you. And it works — they leave steadier, held. The trouble is you have no memory of picking any of this up. The caretaker role arrived the way a season arrives, and the person inside it is running on empty and calling that the shape of things.

So take a load off your own hands. Not all of it — one duty that's outlived its reason, that you carry because stopping seemed like a small betrayal. Set it down on purpose. The ones who leaned on you can find their own feet, and your hands come back to you. Both of you are better for it.
cells.sheetLine: You didn't sign for it, and still you hold it.
